editorialStandard: Documented season narrative. All scorelines and matches are verified against the canonical matchup ledger; 2016–2017 postseason scores are multiweek aggregates. No invented quotes, player performances or locker-room claims.

seasons.title: The First Name on the Trophy
seasons.dek: Before there was a dynasty, there was a third seed that refused to leave the opening season quietly.

sections.heading: The beginning
sections.text: The inaugural Fellas season did not announce Thommy as the league’s inevitable champion. His team opened with losses to Koble and Evans, and three of its first four games ended in defeat. Meanwhile, Halderman set the regular-season pace at 8–4–1. If the league was searching for its first powerhouse, the standings pointed somewhere other than Thommy.

sections.heading: How the season turned
sections.text: What followed was less a runaway than a stubborn recovery. Thommy won four straight games from Weeks 5 through 8, beating Stew, Halderman, Stover and Schermerhorn. There were still setbacks—including a 153–107 loss to Evans in Week 9 and a defeat to Stilly in Week 11—but Thommy survived the schedule at 7–5–1. A 121–121 tie with Halderman in the regular-season finale foreshadowed the matchup awaiting him at the end.

sections.heading: The road to the championship
sections.text: Thommy entered the four-team playoffs as the No. 3 seed. His first assignment was Evans, who had beaten him twice in the regular season. The postseason changed the result: Thommy won the two-week semifinal 227–153. Halderman, the top seed and regular-season leader, waited in the championship. In another two-week aggregate, Thommy scored 223 to Halderman’s 175 and claimed the league’s inaugural title.

sections.heading: Why it still matters
sections.text: The first Fellas champion was not its best regular-season team. He was the manager who changed the outcome when the bracket opened, beating the opponent who had owned the head-to-head matchup and then the team that had led the standings. Every championship story since 2016 has been measured against that first lesson: the trophy belongs to the team that finishes the job.

seasons.title: The Champion Becomes the Standard
seasons.dek: A No. 1 seed, two playoff victories, and the first repeat title in Fellas history.

sections.heading: The burden of the crown
sections.text: Winning the league once made Thommy its original champion. Winning it again required carrying the expectation. He opened 2017 with four straight victories, including a 114–107 win over Evans in Week 4, before an uneven middle of the schedule brought defeats to Stover, Stilly and Schermerhorn. By season’s end he was 8–4, good for the No. 1 seed in the four-team championship bracket.

sections.heading: The decisive stretch
sections.text: The most convincing regular-season answer came in Week 9. Thommy put up 148 against Birch’s 63, an 85-point win that showed how far his offense could separate from an opponent. He closed with victories over Koble and Stew in Weeks 11 and 12, scoring 137 in the regular-season finale. The champion was entering December with both a top seed and momentum.

sections.heading: Two opponents, two tests
sections.text: Evans had beaten Thommy in the inaugural season but lost the 2016 semifinal. The rematch in the 2017 playoff semifinal was much tighter. Thommy won the two-week aggregate 233–217, a 16-point escape. In the final, he met Schermerhorn—the manager who had beaten him 124–90 in Week 7. Thommy reversed that result with a 241–212 championship victory across two weeks.

sections.heading: The meaning of two
sections.text: The repeat changed the league’s history before it had much history at all. The 2016 trophy could be explained as a postseason surge from the third seed; the 2017 championship came from the top of the bracket. Thommy had now shown two different ways to win, and the Fellas had its first dynasty in progress.

seasons.title: Three in a Row, by Inches
seasons.dek: The third championship came without the best record and with almost no margin for error.

sections.heading: A vulnerable defending champion
sections.text: Thommy entered 2018 with two titles and finished the regular season 7–6. Tony led the league at 8–5, and Thommy had endured a series of sharp defeats: Birch beat him 141.84–83.08 in Week 2, Stilly won by nearly 40 in Week 8, and Mitch held him to 73.02 in a Week 13 loss. This was not a title defense built on uninterrupted control.

sections.heading: The first close call
sections.text: Seeded fourth in a six-team playoff field, Thommy had to play an extra round. His opening matchup against Kuhl was decided 96.54–92.64—a 3.90-point margin. It was the kind of win that leaves no room for a grand theory about dominance. One additional lineup play could have ended the attempt at a three-peat immediately.

sections.heading: Through the bracket
sections.text: Tony, the regular-season leader, was next. Thommy won the semifinal 94.80–82.30 and advanced to face Birch, whose Week 2 rout had been one of the defender’s worst regular-season results. The championship was close from start to finish: Thommy 111.58, Birch 106.62. The final margin was 4.96 points. Across all three postseason games, Thommy survived by a combined 21.36.

sections.heading: The three-peat
sections.text: Three championships in the first three seasons is the kind of achievement a league can spend a decade trying to equal. Yet the third was arguably the most fragile: three playoff games, two decided by fewer than five points, and a regular season scarcely above .500. Thommy did not win 2018 by making the season look easy. He won because every close elimination game ended with his name on the right side.

seasons.title: Hogan’s Heroes Finish the Job
seasons.dek: A devastating 11–2 regular season became Birch’s first championship after a final decided by 4.72 points.

sections.heading: From contender to frontrunner
sections.text: Birch had reached the 2018 championship game and come up short against Thommy. The response in 2019 was immediate. He opened by scoring 169.32 against Tony, then won the next five games as well. His first loss did not come until Week 7, against Koble. By the regular-season finish Birch was 11–2, the league’s No. 1 seed, and its clearest front-runner.

sections.heading: The strength of the run
sections.text: The schedule was not without resistance. Kuhl pushed Birch to 146.76–140.04 in Week 3; Stew lost their first matchup 117.24–108.84 in Week 5. After consecutive losses to Koble and Stover in Weeks 7 and 8, Birch answered with five consecutive victories. The response included a 147.94–75.00 rout of Stilly and a 153.74–80.52 defeat of Tony. He had absorbed the only real midseason stumble and reclaimed control.

sections.heading: The two wins that mattered most
sections.text: The top seed advanced to the semifinal, where Tony—already beaten twice by Birch in the regular season—stood between Hogan’s Heroes and another title game. Birch scored 153.10 in a 21.58-point victory. The final was against Stew, a manager Birch had beaten by 8.40 in Week 5. It would be closer still: Birch 114.14, Stew 109.42. The championship was settled by 4.72 points.

sections.heading: The answer to 2018
sections.text: A year earlier, Birch had watched the trophy go to Thommy. In 2019, he turned a league-best regular season into a title instead of another almost. The franchise would finish third in both 2020 and 2021, extending its stretch among the league’s best. But 2019 remains the peak: an 11-win campaign followed by two playoff victories that finally put Hogan’s Heroes on the championship line.

seasons.title: The Sixth Seed Takes the Trophy
seasons.dek: Koble’s improbable title run was built on surviving a 7–7 season and beating the league’s best when it counted.

sections.heading: No favorite on paper
sections.text: Koble was 7–7 in the 2020 regular season, good for the sixth and final playoff seed. Mitch, at 9–4, stood atop the field; Birch, also 9–4, had the other first-round bye. Koble’s year had been wildly uneven. He scored 143.34 in a Week 6 demolition of Mitch, then lost five of his next seven games, including a 121.30–50.58 defeat to Tony in Week 10.

sections.heading: Getting into the fight
sections.text: A Week 12 win over Stilly and a Week 14 victory over Kuhl helped keep Koble alive. A sixth seed does not receive the luxury of waiting for the field to thin. The archive verifies that he came through the opening playoff round, although the recovered game ledger does not provide a complete score for that matchup. It does establish what happened next: a semifinal against Birch.

sections.heading: The favorites fall
sections.text: Koble put up 130.42 against Birch’s 82.82 in Week 15, knocking out the second seed by 47.60 points. That set up a final against Mitch, the top seed and a manager Koble had both crushed and struggled against over the course of the year’s uneven results. In Week 16 Koble won 117.48–99.42, an 18.06-point championship margin.

sections.heading: The lesson of the sixth seed
sections.text: Koble did not need a dominant regular season to win the only games that could put him on the trophy. The 2020 championship stands as the classic argument for the playoff bracket: qualify, survive, and be better than the favorite on the day that decides it. It is the league’s first documented championship by a No. 6 seed.

seasons.title: Tony Wins the One That Counts
seasons.dek: Ten regular-season wins, an active front office, and a championship final decided by just 4.30 points.

sections.heading: A contender returns
sections.text: After going 4–10 in 2020, Tony began 2021 by beating Birch and then won five of his first seven games. His offense broke open the season with consecutive strong performances: 167.14 points against Thommy in Week 6 and 151.46 against Kuhl in Week 7. By the end he was 10–3, the No. 2 seed and a first-round bye recipient behind Birch’s 11–2 regular-season club.

sections.heading: The roster takes shape
sections.text: The transaction record shows a manager willing to make meaningful changes. In October, Tony acquired Joe Mixon from Koble in exchange for Zack Moss and James Robinson. A later deal sent Kareem Hunt to Stilly for CeeDee Lamb, and another trade brought Kyle Pitts Sr. from Kuhl for Jarvis Landry and George Kittle. Those are documented moves, not proof that any single trade decided the championship. Together, they show how actively Tony reshaped his options in a winning season.

sections.heading: The road to the final
sections.text: With the opening playoff bye secured, Tony faced Stover in the semifinal. The result was 94.96–73.44, a 21.52-point win. The final opponent was Evans, who had played Tony twice during the regular season. Tony had won both of those games, including a 151.36–80.08 decision in Week 12. The championship rematch was nothing like that rout: Tony 138.28, Evans 133.98.

sections.heading: A narrow margin, a permanent title
sections.text: A difference of 4.30 points separated Tony’s first championship from a runner-up finish. The trophy capped a 10-win regular season and marked a return from the previous year’s losing record. For Tony, 2021 is the season where sustained contention and active roster management finally ended with the result everyone remembers: champion.

seasons.title: Stover Settles the Score
seasons.dek: The league’s highest-scoring regular-season team reached the final. Stover made sure it didn’t win.

sections.heading: The challenger
sections.text: Stew went 11–3 and led the 2022 regular season, but Stover was not far behind. His 9–5 record earned the No. 2 seed and a first-round bye. The season had been marked by difficult matchups: Stew beat Stover 159.72–119.60 in Week 2, and Kuhl, Evans and Stilly also handed him regular-season losses. The standings favored Stew. The head-to-head season series was split.

sections.heading: Proof of a response
sections.text: The second meeting with Stew arrived in Week 11. Stover scored 137.62 and won by 27.82, reversing the result of the early-season defeat. He closed the regular season with a 104.18–60.66 victory over Tony in Week 14. The late schedule had losses too, but he entered the bracket as one of its two bye teams with evidence he could beat the favorite.

sections.heading: December belongs to Stover
sections.text: Kuhl awaited in the semifinal, and Stover won 112.56–87.68. The final brought the matchup the league’s standings had anticipated: Stew, the 11-win No. 1 seed, against Stover, the No. 2 seed. There was no suspense in the final margin. Stover scored 99.22; Stew managed 48.16. The 51.06-point victory transformed a competitive season series into a decisive championship result.

sections.heading: The title that defined Gurt
sections.text: Stover’s previous campaign had included an 11–3 regular season without the trophy. In 2022 he completed what that earlier contender could not. The Fellas title did not go to the team with the league’s best record or scoring résumé; it went to the manager who won the last meeting. For the franchise remembered as Gurt, 2022 became the championship season.

seasons.title: From 0–4 to Fellas Champion
seasons.dek: Stilly’s first four games were losses. His last three were the wins that mattered most.

sections.heading: A season in trouble
sections.text: Four weeks into 2023, Stilly had no wins. Mitch, Stew, Tony and Stover had each beaten him, and there was no evidence in the standings that a title run was coming. Week 5 brought the first breakthrough: a 127.36–98.72 win over Evans. Stilly remained uneven into October, including another loss to Koble and a Week 10 defeat to Mitch. The season was still being earned, not handed to him.

sections.heading: The roster and the surge
sections.text: On October 26, Stilly traded Cooper Kupp to Tony for Mike Evans and Derrick Henry. The ledger confirms the exchange; it cannot by itself prove how much of the championship came from the deal. The measurable turnaround is clearer. Stilly won four consecutive regular-season games from Weeks 11–14, including a 173.86–99.58 rout of Tony in Week 12 and a 159.66–89.10 victory over Stover in Week 13. The club that started 0–4 finished 8–6 and entered the bracket as the No. 4 seed.

sections.heading: Three games to forever
sections.text: There was no bye and no easy shortcut. Stilly beat Birch 146.36–105.06 in the opening round. Next came Tony, the 10–4 regular-season leader and the trade partner from October; Stilly won the semifinal 141.66–108.58. The final brought Mitch, who had beaten Stilly twice during the regular season. This time the result flipped. Stilly scored 104.96 to Mitch’s 90.18, winning the championship by 14.78 points.

sections.heading: The comeback that earned a ring
sections.text: A first Fellas championship after an 0–4 opening is more than a turnaround in the standings. Stilly survived the early schedule, built momentum late, and beat two opponents in the playoffs who had given him trouble in the regular season. The October trade is a chapter in the story; the four-game late surge and three playoff victories are the proof of how the season ended.

seasons.title: The Fourth Ring, Six Years Later
seasons.dek: Thommy returned to the top by surviving the semifinal and overwhelming the champion in the final.

sections.heading: A dynasty from another era
sections.text: Thommy had won the league’s first three championships, then spent five seasons without another. By 2024, the three-peat belonged to Fellas history rather than the current playoff conversation. His season began with six straight victories, including a 152.02–79.78 result against Tony in Week 6. Even four losses in the final eight regular-season weeks could not undo the foundation. Thommy finished 9–5 and claimed the No. 2 seed and a bye.

sections.heading: The test he nearly failed
sections.text: The playoff semifinal against JMid was the hinge of the entire campaign. JMid had led the league in regular-season points scored and had beaten Thommy in Week 7, 107.24–103.80. Their postseason rematch was closer still. Thommy escaped 123.38–121.08, a margin of just 2.30 points. Had one play broken differently, there would have been no fourth-ring story.

sections.heading: One final, one exclamation point
sections.text: Stilly, the defending 2023 champion, waited in the title game. The rivals had split their two regular-season meetings: Thommy won in Week 1 and Stilly took the Week 10 rematch. But the championship was one-sided. Thommy put up 205.30 against Stilly’s 114.88, a 90.42-point margin that stands in stark contrast to the semifinal escape.

sections.heading: The return
sections.text: Thommy had already written the league’s first dynasty. The 2024 title gave that career a second defining era. It arrived not through another undefeated march but through a narrow escape followed by a historic final statement. Six years separated his third and fourth rings. No one else in the current league had that many, and the original champion had proved the story was not finished.

seasons.title: Scott’s Fast Track to the Trophy
seasons.dek: One season after a 5–9 debut, Scott beat the finalists by a combined 141.80 points.

sections.heading: The sophomore leap
sections.text: Scott’s first Fellas season ended 5–9 in 2024. The next year was different, though not perfectly smooth. He opened 2025 with three straight wins, including a 113.52–112.54 escape against Stover in Week 3, then lost to Thommy and Stilly in consecutive weeks. The title favorite was elsewhere: Mitch finished 13–1. Scott made the playoffs at 8–6 as the No. 2 seed, earning a first-round bye despite the uneven record.

sections.heading: The run takes shape
sections.text: The middle of the schedule supplied a glimpse of what Scott could do when the scoring came together: 154.76 points in a Week 6 win over Stew. Week 7 brought a 180.86–136.06 loss to Mitch, a reminder that the league’s regular-season giant remained ahead. But Scott answered later with a 155.10–53.72 rout of JMid in Week 11, a 101.38-point victory. He did not finish with the most wins; he arrived at the postseason with proven scoring upside.

sections.heading: A playoff demolition
sections.text: The first-round bye put Scott directly into a semifinal against Birch. Scott scored 141.88 while Birch managed 70.40, a 71.48-point victory. The final opponent was Thommy, the four-time champion, who had beaten Scott 165.50–130.74 in Week 4. The championship reversed that result decisively. Scott scored 156.32 to Thommy’s 86.00, winning by 70.32 points.

sections.heading: An arrival nobody could miss
sections.text: Scott’s two postseason wins totaled a 141.80-point advantage. In his second season, he had gone from a losing debut to a champion whose final two games left no doubt about the outcome. The 2025 trophy is a reminder that a league’s most dominant regular-season team does not automatically write its final chapter. Scott did.
